newsitem.title: UK: BRITAIN TO RUN GRAND NATIONAL AFTER BOMB SCARE.
newsitem.headline: BRITAIN TO RUN GRAND NATIONAL AFTER BOMB SCARE.

text.p: The 150th Grand National, the premier horse race in Britain's sporting calendar, will be re-staged on Monday after a suspected IRA bomb scare wrecked the original race, police said on Sunday.
"I am delighted that we are going to run the world's greatest steeplechase tomorrow," said Charles Barnett, managing director of Aintree race course in northewst England.
Spectators would be allowed free entry to the stands when the race is run at 5:00 pm (1600 GMT).

The announcement came one day after telephoned bomb warnings forced the abandonment of the race, which is watched by 250 million television viewers around the world, and the evacuation of 70,000 people.
On Sunday, Aintree staff were working flat out to prepare the course. Police continued to search the thousands of cars still stranded as disappointed racegoers milled around.
Police Assistant Chief Constable Paul Stephenson said no bombs had been found but the search was continuing.
"No one has yet claimed responsibility for the bomb threats and we can all draw our own conclusions from that," he said.

Prime Minister John Major said he had "no doubt" the Irish Republican Army (IRA), fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland, was to blame for the spectacular bomb scare, warning that such disruptions would only hinder the peace process.
"These people are murderers. They have murdered before. They will murder again, and people ought not to take these threats lightly," Major told BBC television.
He said such attacks, following a spate of similar scares at major road and rail points, would only hurt efforts by the IRA's political allies Sinn Fein to get back into the peace talks.

In Liverpool more than 2,000 people were forced to spend Saturday night sleeping on floors next to strangers, in hostels and leisure centres, wherever they could find an empty corner out of the blustery weather.
One couple slept in a hotel sauna, another racegoer in the stable boys' hostel on the course.
"The public were ringing in with offers," said an employee at Liverpool's social services department. "I think some pubs and clubs were open all night to try and help out."
Princess Anne, horse-loving daughter of Queen Elizabeth, and Oscar-winning actor Gregory Peck, were among the punters who fell victim to one of the biggest evaucations in sports history.
Twenty-four hours after the security scare, motorists were finally allowed back to the Aintree car parks on Sunday to recover their vehicles.
An estimated 7,000 cars and coaches were trapped overnight while each one was checked individually. Police said any cars not claimed by midnight on Sunday would be towed away.

Increased security measures were expected at Anfield soccer ground nearby where Liverpool played Coventry City on Sunday in a Premier League match, and at Wembley stadium in north London for the League Cup final.
"Our advice to fans is to be extra vigilant, the same sort of advice we give to anyone in London in the current climate of possible terrorist activity," said a police spokesman in London.
Police carried out three controlled explosions on suspicious objects after the coded bomb warnings at Aintree, but all proved harmless.
Major warned Britain that the lack of actual bombs or injuries should not lead to complacency.
"There's a great danger that people will be lulled into a false sense of security and then there will be a bomb," Major said on BBC television's Breakfast with Frost show.
With many Britons long used to security alerts and bomb scares, the chief concern of many race-goers was their bets.
An estimated $120 million is bet on the National and bookmakers said bets would stand for Monday's 1600 GMT re-run.
Home (Interior) Secretary Michael Howard said he was "absolutely delighted" the race would be going ahead.
"It is proof that terrorist action such as we saw yesterday is completely futile," he said.
